title: Twelve guesses at Rome
hook: Astronomers and mapmakers spent centuries on one short distance. How close did they get?

knows: latitude and longitude locate a place
doesNotKnow: that the errors ran almost all one way and were huge even for a short, well-travelled distance, because longitude needed time

misconception: Old estimates scattered around the truth, so their average was about right.
objective: The learner can say that all twelve pre-1644 estimates of the Toledo-Rome longitude difference put Rome too far east (only one within 2 degrees; the middle one about 780 km too far), that longitude was hard because it needs a difference in local time, and that this record does not explain why every error ran east.

claims.text: Latitude can be read from the Sun or a star, but longitude needs the difference in local time between two places (one hour = 15 degrees).
claims.source: Convention: 360 degrees / 24 hours = 15 degrees per hour (geography:sun-time-from-longitude). Brief 6 claim (4).
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation checked: local solar time changes by 360/24 = 15 degrees of longitude per hour of the Earth's turn, so a longitude difference is a local-time difference; latitude follows from the altitude of the Sun or the pole star. Geometry, not a cited fact.

recall.question: Two clocks: one set to noon where you are, one to noon at your home port. They differ by 2 hours. How far east or west are you?
recall.why: The Earth turns 15 degrees an hour, so a 2-hour difference in local time is 30 degrees of longitude. Without a way to compare times, longitude could not be measured well.
